json.reasoning: True issue, and it lives in the SPEC (a), not the code. The spec's three ensures all reference only the mutated original `stake` (staked_sui_amount/pool_id/stake_activation_epoch of `stake`). The newly created object returned by `stake.split(split_amount, ctx)` is consumed immediately by `transfer::transfer(..., ctx.sender())` and is never bound to a spec-visible variable, so none of its three properties (principal==split_amount, pool_id==old, stake_activation_epoch==old) are constrained. The declared ghost vars SpecTransferAddress / SpecTransferAddressExists are never referenced in any ensures, so even the fact and recipient of the transfer go unverified. Exactly 3 of the 6 writeup ensures — the entire output half, including the conservation invariant (two principals summing to the original) — are unproven. I ruled out (b) by reading staking_pool::split in sources/staking_pool.move: the constructor sets `pool_id: self.pool_id`, `stake_activation_epoch: self.stake_activation_epoch`, and `principal: self.principal.split(split_amount)` (balance::split returns exactly split_amount and reduces self by that amount), so all three required properties hold and the original-side aborts/invariants the spec already proves are consistent with it. The code is correct; tightening the spec would close the coverage gap, not expose a defect. Severity is high because the unverified portion is the function's entire purpose (the transferred split receipt) plus principal conservation on a financial staking primitive — a future regression in split() (e.g. wrong pool_id or doubled principal) would pass silently. Verifying it requires ghost-object infrastructure to capture the transferred object's fields, which the current spec lacks.
